title: Hustle Cream — Snarky Scan-It Tech Brief
description: A warm-cream newsletter layout engineered for editorial irreverence: a display pun headline commands the top, a meme-style illustration anchors the right, three skimmable story blurbs stack the left, and a mustard sponsor strip closes the bottom with hard contrast.
philosophy: This template exists because most newsletter slides are either sterile infographics or glorified bullet dumps — neither has a personality. It values editorial voice over visual neutrality, the kind of layout that reads like a punchline before delivering the actual news. It refuses harmonious minimalism in favor of structured attitude: bold type, conversational copy weight, and a sponsor strip that earns its rent. Built for writers who have opinions and readers who skim on a coffee break.
goodFor: Weekly tech newsletter roundups with a conversational, irreverent editorial tone
Sponsor-forward media decks where bottom-strip placement and contrast must pop
Three-story summary formats paired with a single illustrated visual anchor
Digitally fluent audiences who expect skimmable, personality-driven content
avoidFor: Formal regulatory or compliance briefings requiring neutral authority
Chart-heavy quarterly financial reviews where data density is primary
Conservative B2B enterprise sales pitches to C-suite stakeholders
Academic or research presentations demanding citation-dense, structured layouts
author: harness

examples.promptCore: The cover should feel like the front page of a cheeky tech zine written by someone who finds most newsletters deeply embarrassing — headline energy is punchline-first, big and slightly unhinged. A loose illustrated character on the right deflates any creeping self-importance, keeping the composition in on the joke. Warm and tactile in atmosphere, channeling risograph-print irreverence over digital polish. Avoid anything that reads as authoritative or harmoniously refined; the charm lives entirely in structured attitude.

examples.layoutNotes: 12-column grid with an 8% outer margin; display headline spans cols 1–12 in the top third, stacked across two lines to maximize typographic impact. A meme-style illustration anchors the right 40% of the mid-zone, edge-bleeding toward the right boundary. Subtitle or issue tagline occupies cols 1–6 in the lower mid-section, establishing a left-rail reading anchor. A full-bleed horizontal strip locks the bottom edge; a small issue-number or date tag pins the top-left corner as a metadata flourish.

examples.promptCore: The slide feels like a newspaper front page that went to a roast — structured enough to trust, irreverent enough to enjoy. The left column pulses with stacked editorial rhythm, three blurbs each landing like a tiny punchline before delivering the actual news, kept honest by crisp rule lines that organize without stiffening. The meme illustration on the right acts as a visual exclamation point, giving the eye somewhere to exhale before looping back into the copy stack. The sponsor strip closes with blunt contrast — a deliberate gear-shift, never decorative. Avoid harmonious softness, rounded friendliness, or anything that whispers committee consensus.

examples.layoutNotes: 12-column grid: story blurbs occupy cols 1–7 as a vertical stack of three cards, each separated by a hairline rule and holding a kicker label, punchy headline fragment, and one-sentence summary. Cols 8–12 host a full-height meme-style illustration bleeding to the right edge with no inner gutter. A high-contrast sponsor strip runs edge-to-edge at the bottom, roughly 13% of slide height, with sponsor copy center- or left-aligned inside it. A display-scale pun headline spans the full width above the two-column split, left-aligned with a compact ~6% outer margin.
